title: Why Do Bridges Have Metal Teeth?
description:
Drive across a big bridge and at some point your car goes over a row of steel teeth, locked together like the fingers of two hands. Thump, thump. Most people never look down. But those teeth are there because the bridge is moving, right now, under your wheels. Today, eleven parts of a bridge, and why each one exists, starting with those metal teeth.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 11 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:05 1. The metal teeth
2:23 2. The joint with many beams
3:35 3. The rubber pads under the deck
4:48 4. The old rocker bearing
5:54 5. The holes in the deck
7:00 6. The riverbed around the pier
8:13 7. The spiral on the cables
9:20 8. The main cable that breathes dry air
10:30 9. The shape of the deck
11:42 10. The bridge that freezes first
12:48 11. The paint that never ends
13:57 The verdict

Sources:
- Expansion joints (finger and modular), thermal expansion of steel ~12e-6 per °C: Wikipedia, "Expansion joint" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expansion_joint ; FHWA, "Bridge Preservation Guide" https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/bridge/preservation/
- Bridge bearings (elastomeric, pot, sliding, rocker, seismic isolation): Wikipedia, "Bridge bearing" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_bearing
- Deck drainage, chlorides and rebar corrosion: FHWA, "Corrosion Protection of Concrete Bridges" https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/
- Scour; Schoharie Creek Bridge collapse (5 April 1987, 10 deaths): NTSB report HAR-88/02 ; Wikipedia, "Schoharie Creek Bridge collapse" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoharie_Creek_Bridge_collapse ; FHWA HEC-18 "Evaluating Scour at Bridges"
- Rain-wind induced vibration of stay cables, helical fillets and dampers: Wikipedia, "Cable-stayed bridge" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable-stayed_bridge ; Hikami & Shiraishi (1988), Journal of Wind Engineering and Industrial Aerodynamics
- Main cable dehumidification (Akashi Kaikyo Bridge): Wikipedia, "Akashi Kaikyō Bridge" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akashi_Kaiky%C5%8D_Bridge ; Honshu-Shikoku Bridge Expressway
- Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse (7 November 1940, ~64 km/h wind, dog Tubby): Wikipedia, "Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_(1940)
- Bridges freeze before roads: US National Weather Service / FHWA Road Weather Management https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/weather/
- Forth Bridge repainting (2002-2011, coating expected to last 25+ years): Wikipedia, "Forth Bridge" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forth_Bridge ; Network Rail
